headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Normal Labour
headings.content: Normal labour, also known as childbirth or parturition, is defined as the physiological process by which the fetus, placenta, and membranes are expelled from the uterus through the vagina. For it to be classified as normal or eutocia, several key criteria must be met: it must be spontaneous in onset, low-risk at the start and remaining so throughout labour, vertex presentation of the fetus, and occurring at term between 37 and 42 completed weeks of gestation. Furthermore, delivery should happen without artificial interventions such as augmentation or instrumental delivery where possible, and it must result in the birth of a healthy infant with a good Apgar score while ensuring the mother remains in good physiological and psychological condition. Understanding this definition is critical for nursing students in Nigeria, as it forms the baseline against which abnormal labour, or dystocia, is recognized and managed in clinical settings like primary health care centers, general hospitals, and tertiary teaching hospitals. Nurses must recognize that labour is dynamic, involving coordinated uterine contractions, effacement and dilatation of the cervix, and descent of the presenting part. Recognizing normal progression helps prevent unnecessary medicalization while staying vigilant for any deviation that threatens maternal or fetal well-being, thereby reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality rates in resource-constrained environments.

headings.title: Stages of Labour and Physiology
headings.content: Labour is divided into four distinct clinical stages, each characterized by specific physiological events and nursing implications. The first stage begins with the onset of true uterine contractions and ends with full cervical dilatation (10 centimeters). It is subdivided into the latent phase (slow cervical change up to 5 cm) and the active phase (rapid cervical change from 5 cm to 10 cm). Physiologically, this stage relies on myometrial contractility, cervical ripening, and retraction. The second stage starts from full cervical dilatation and ends with the complete expulsion of the fetus. During this stage, maternal pushing efforts, augmented by involuntary uterine contractions, facilitate the descent and birth of the baby. Cardinal movements of the labour mechanism—such as engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, and external rotation—occur predominantly during the first and second stages. The third stage spans from the birth of the baby until the complete expulsion of the placenta and fetal membranes, driven by uterine retraction and controlled placental separation. The fourth stage refers to the immediate postpartum period, lasting up to two hours after placental delivery, where physiological stabilization, observation for postpartum hemorrhage, and initiation of maternal-neonatal bonding take place. As nursing students, mastering these stages allows you to anticipate physiological shifts, provide timely interventions, and evaluate maternal and fetal progress accurately during intrapartum care.

headings.title: Admission Assessment and Initial Evaluation
headings.content: The admission assessment and initial evaluation of a parturient are crucial procedures that set the tone for intrapartum management. When a pregnant woman arrives in the labour ward, the nurse must conduct a comprehensive, respectful, and systematic evaluation. This begins with a detailed history taking: noting maternal age, parity, gestational age, history of previous pregnancies, medical-surgical history, details of the current pregnancy, and the exact history of present labour (onset, frequency, and intensity of contractions, and presence or absence of a bloody show or rupture of membranes). Following history taking, a general physical and systemic examination is performed, including taking vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and respiration) and checking for lower limb edema or pallor. Abdominal examination follows Leopold's maneuvers to determine fetal lie, presentation, position, and degree of descent, alongside auscultating the fetal heart rate (FHR) using a Pinard stethoscope or Doppler. A sterile speculum or digital vaginal examination is performed, with appropriate consent, to assess cervical effacement, dilatation, membrane status, and pelvic adequacy. Laboratory investigations such as urinalysis for protein and glucose, and checking hemoglobin status, are completed. Finally, the nurse analyzes these findings to determine whether the woman is truly in labour, admits her, and commences continuous supportive care while reassuring her and her birth companion.

headings.title: First Stage of Labour: Monitoring and Care
headings.content: Monitoring and care during the first stage of labour require continuous vigilance, empathy, and evidence-based nursing interventions. The primary goals are to ensure maternal-fetal well-being, monitor the progress of labour, and provide holistic comfort measures. Maternal vital signs—blood pressure, pulse, and temperature—must be monitored regularly (e.g., blood pressure every 4 hours, pulse every 30 to 60 minutes) to detect early signs of distress, dehydration, or infection. Fetal well-being is assessed by auscultating the fetal heart rate every 30 minutes during the active phase, ideally immediately after a contraction, for at least one full minute. Regular assessment of contraction frequency, duration, and strength is documented. The nurse should encourage adequate hydration through oral fluids (water or clear isotonic drinks) unless contraindications exist, and promote mobility and optimal maternal positions such as left lateral or upright positions to enhance uterine perfusion and fetal descent. Pain management is an integral component of care; non-pharmacological methods such as back rubs, warm baths, breathing exercises, and continuous emotional support by a birth companion significantly reduce anxiety and pain perception. Urine output should be monitored, and bladder distension prevented by encouraging frequent voiding. Vaginal examinations are performed judiciously (usually every 4 hours) to avoid introducing infection while tracking progress. Any abnormal findings, such as thick meconium-stained liquor, abnormal fetal heart rates, or maternal pyrexia, must be reported immediately to the attending midwife or obstetrician.

headings.title: Second Stage of Labour: Conduct of Delivery
headings.content: The second stage of labour demands skilled nursing and midwifery conduct to ensure a safe delivery for both mother and baby. Once the cervix is fully dilated, preparations for delivery must be finalized, including assembling sterile delivery packs, checking resuscitation equipment, and ensuring personal protective equipment is worn. The nurse provides continuous encouragement, coaching the mother on effective pushing techniques during contractions while advising relaxation between contractions to prevent maternal exhaustion and fetal hypoxia. Maternal positioning can be individualized; semi-recumbent, squatting, or side-lying positions are effective, avoiding prolonged supine positions which can cause aortocaval compression and fetal distress. As the fetal head crowns, the nurse protects the perineum using controlled maneuvers (such as Ritgen's maneuver) to prevent severe perineal tears. Once the head is delivered, the nurse checks for nuchal cords around the neck; if present, they are gently slipped over the head or clamped and cut if tight. The anterior shoulder is guided down, followed by the posterior shoulder, and the rest of the baby's body is delivered smoothly. Immediate newborn care follows: placing the baby on the mother's abdomen for skin-to-skin contact, drying and stimulating the baby, clearing the airway if necessary, assessing breathing and heart rate, and assigning the Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes. Throughout this critical stage, vigilance, calm communication, and prompt intervention are paramount.

headings.title: Third Stage of Labour: Active Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage (AMTSL)
headings.content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is a leading cause of maternal mortality in Nigeria and globally, making Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL) an essential, life-saving competency for all nursing and midwifery students. AMTSL consists of three core interventions administered immediately after the birth of the baby to prevent PPH primarily caused by uterine atony. The first step is the administration of a uterotonic drug within one minute of delivery; oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly (or intravenously) is the gold standard because it has rapid onset and minimal side effects. The second step is controlled cord traction (CCT), which involves applying gentle traction on the umbilical cord while simultaneously performing counter-pressure (suprapubic sign/Brandt-Andrews maneuver) on the uterus once signs of placental separation are evident (uterine hardening, lengthening of the cord, and a gush of blood). The third step is uterine massage; immediately after the placenta is delivered, the nurse must massage the uterine fundus through the abdominal wall until it remains contracted and firm. Additional components include inspecting the placenta and membranes to ensure completeness and examining the birth canal for lacerations. Practicing AMTSL systematically reduces the incidence of PPH by over 60%, safeguarding maternal survival in clinical practice.

headings.title: Fourth Stage of Labour and Immediate Postpartum Care
headings.content: The fourth stage of labour encompasses the immediate postpartum period, typically defined as the first two hours following the delivery of the placenta. This is a critical transition window during which the mother is at the highest physiological risk for sudden postpartum hemorrhage, uterine subinvolution, and cardiovascular instability. Nursing care during this phase focuses on rigorous monitoring and supportive comfort. The nurse must check maternal vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, and temperature) every 15 minutes for the first hour, and every 30 minutes during the second hour. Palpation of the uterine fundus is equally frequent to ensure it remains well-contracted, hard, and midline. The nurse must inspect the amount, color, and consistency of vaginal bleeding (lochia rubra) and check for the presence of clots. Perineal care is provided, assessing any episiotomy or tear repair for hematoma formation, excessive swelling, or active bleeding. Bladder function must be monitored, encouraging spontaneous voiding since a distended bladder can displace the uterus and precipitate PPH. Beyond physical monitoring, the fourth stage is foundational for promoting family bonding and early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour of life, leveraging the newborn's alert state. The nurse also provides emotional reassurance, pain relief, and nutritional support, ensuring the mother transitions safely from the labour unit to the postnatal ward.

headings.title: Documentation and Partograph Utilization
headings.content: Documentation and partograph utilization are indispensable tools for safe, high-quality intrapartum care. The partograph is a pictorial overview of labour that serves as an early-warning system to detect abnormal progress, prevent prolonged and obstructed labour, and reduce maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. Endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO), the partograph charts fetal heart rate, amniotic fluid status, cervical dilatation, descent of the head, uterine contractions, oxytocin administration, medications given, and maternal vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, and temperature). It features two critical lines on the cervical dilatation graph: the alert line, which starts at 4 cm of dilatation and represents the rate of labour progress of the slowest 10% of primigravidae, and the action line, which is parallel and 4 hours to the right of the alert line. If the plotted cervical dilatation crosses to the right of the alert line, it indicates potential delay, and the woman must be transferred to a facility with comprehensive emergency obstetric care if she is at a primary level. Crossing the action line mandates immediate medical evaluation and active intervention. In addition to the partograph, comprehensive nursing documentation requires accurate, contemporaneous recording of all assessments, interventions, medication administrations, and patient communications in the nursing notes. For nursing students, mastering the partograph is mandatory for passing professional licensing exams and delivering safe clinical care across Nigerian health institutions.
